sections.title: Measure the footprint
sections.text: Note the length and width of clear floor, which is usually smaller than the room itself. A standing curl needs fairly little space, while a walking lunge or a floor exercise may need room to stretch out your arms and legs. Leave extra space around moving weights and think about how the exercise starts and ends.

sections.title: Think in three dimensions
sections.text: A squat or standing row needs room to the sides for your elbows and the equipment. A push-up or dead bug needs floor space as long as your body. A kettlebell swing needs open space in front, behind and around the bell, and overhead presses or jumps need vertical room.

sections.title: Hidden obstacles
sections.text: Watch for low tables, hanging lights, sharp corners, heaters, pets, cables, rugs and doors that open into your area. Check that the floor is still non-slip once your mat is down. If you can only just finish one rep without touching furniture, the space is too tight for a full workout.

sections.title: A plan for small spaces
sections.text: In a narrow space, do stationary split squats in place of walking lunges, and seated or floor-based upper-body work in place of big side-to-side movements. If the room is too small for loaded carries, do anti-lateral-flexion exercises on the spot. Keep the movement pattern and let the specific exercise change.

sections.title: Using TrainUp
sections.text: Enter your floor size and ceiling height in Profile. The plan then picks only exercises whose movement, including the equipment, fits that space.
